title: Squint : Extraocular Muscles and Binocular Single Vision

questions.sec: Squint — definition, overview and causes
questions.q: Squint per the book is a:
questions.exp: Squint: deviation from binocular vision. (Book p43)

questions.sec: Squint — definition, overview and causes
questions.q: Fill up: the overview of squint in the book is deviation of direction of ______ in one/both eyes and impairment in ocular movement.
questions.exp: Overview: deviation of direction of vessels in one/both eyes and impairment in ocular movement. (Book p43)

questions.sec: Squint — definition, overview and causes
questions.q: All of the following are listed musclar disorder causes of squint in the book EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Muscular disorders: myasthenia gravis, atrophy, dystrophy; cranial nerve lesions give the rest. (Book p43)

questions.sec: Squint — definition, overview and causes
questions.q: Match the cranial nerve with the muscle it supplies in the book — 1) CN IV 2) CN VI 3) CN III … A) Lateral rectus B) Other extraocular muscles C) Superior oblique
questions.exp: CN IV supplies superior oblique; CN VI supplies lateral rectus; CN III supplies other extraocular muscles (mnemonic SO4LR6O3). (Book p43)

questions.sec: EOM — anatomical actions and the clinical action rule
questions.q: Per the book, anatomical actions of the EOM are the ability to be free from neural control, based on:
opts: The direction of the blood supply
questions.exp: Anatomical actions: ability to be free from neural control; based on direction of tendons. (Book p43)

questions.sec: EOM — anatomical actions and the clinical action rule
questions.q: Match the muscle with its primary (1°) action in the book's table — 1) Superior rectus 2) Inferior rectus 3) Superior oblique 4) Inferior oblique … A) Intorsion B) Elevation C) Depression D) Extorsion
questions.exp: 1° actions: SR — elevation; IR — depression; SO — intorsion; IO — extorsion. (Book p43)

questions.sec: EOM — anatomical actions and the clinical action rule
questions.q: The book's 3° actions of the recti and obliques include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: 3° actions: adduction (SR and IR), abduction (SO and IO); 2° actions are intorsion (SR), extorsion (IR), depression (SO), elevation (IO). The lateral rectus has no intorsion action. (Book p43)

questions.sec: EOM — anatomical actions and the clinical action rule
questions.q: Fill up: the clinically invisible ocular movements in the book are intorsion (inward/nasal rotation) and ______ (outward/temporal rotation).
questions.exp: Clinically visible: adduction, abduction, elevation, depression; clinically invisible: intorsion (inward/nasal rotation), extorsion (outward/temporal rotation). (Book p43)

questions.sec: EOM — anatomical actions and the clinical action rule
questions.q: The rule for clinical actions in the book is: 1° actions predominate in the ______ eye.
questions.exp: Rule: 1° actions predominate in the abducted eye; 2° actions predominate in the adducted eye. Use: to test actions of individual muscles. (Book p43)

questions.sec: EOM — anatomical actions and the clinical action rule
questions.q: Which statement about single-eye actions in the book's table is FALSE?
opts: Levator palpebrae superioris: elevation of the upper eyelid
questions.exp: SO's 1° action is intorsion (2° depression, 3° abduction); LPS elevates the upper eyelid; MR adducts; LR abducts. (Book p43)

questions.sec: Visual and orbital axes — why SR is a pure elevator
questions.q: Per the book's visual and orbital axes diagram, the visual axis makes an angle of ______ with the orbital axis, and the SR/IR muscle axes run parallel to the orbital axis at ______ with the sagittal plane.
questions.exp: Visual axis–orbital axis 23°; SR and IR–muscle axes parallel to the orbital axis at 23° with the sagittal plane; LR–muscle axis −45° with the sagittal plane; MR axis parallel to the sagittal plane. (Book p44)

questions.sec: Visual and orbital axes — why SR is a pure elevator
questions.q: When the eye abducts by 23°, the visual axis and the SR's orbital axis coincide. Per the book the consequence is:
opts: Vertical action predominates, making the SR a pure elevator
The SR acts as a pure depressor in that position
The SR loses all its action in that position
The LR becomes the pure elevator in that position
questions.exp: If the eye abducts by 23°, the visual axis and the muscle orbital axis coincide → vertical action predominates → SR → pure elevator. (Book p44)

questions.sec: Visual and orbital axes — why SR is a pure elevator
questions.q: Match the clinical function in the book's diagram with its muscle — 1) Pure elevation 2) Pure depression 3) Elevation in abduction 4) Depression in abduction … A) SO B) SR + IO C) SO + IR D) SR
questions.exp: Pure elevation: SR + IO; pure depression: SO + IR; elevation in abduction: SR; depression in abduction: SO. (Book p44)

questions.sec: Binocular single vision — grades and formation
questions.q: Binocular single vision (BSV) per the book is the:
opts: Loss of fusion of the two images
Formation of a composite image using both eyes
questions.exp: BSV: formation of a composite image using both the eyes. (Book p44)

questions.sec: Binocular single vision — grades and formation
questions.q: Match the BSV grade with its definition in the book — 1) Grade 1 2) Grade 2 3) Grade 3 … A) Stereopsis, binocular depth perception B) Simultaneous macular perception C) Fusion of similar images with minute retinal differences
questions.exp: Grade 1: simultaneous macular perception; Grade 2: fusion of similar images with minute retinal differences; Grade 3: stereopsis, binocular depth perception. (Book p44)

questions.sec: Binocular single vision — grades and formation
questions.q: Fill up: synergistic muscles in the book are 2 muscles with the same action in the same eye, e.g. right SR + right IO (both cause ______).
questions.exp: Synergistic muscles: 2 muscles with the same action in the same eye — eg right SR + right IO (both cause elevation). (Book p44)

questions.sec: Binocular single vision — grades and formation
questions.q: Yoke muscles (CN synergists) in the book are a pair of muscles, one from each eye, enabling both eyeballs to move in the same direction — a ______ movement.
questions.exp: Yoke muscles/CN synergists: a pair of muscles, one from each eye, enabling both eyeballs to move in the same direction — version movement. (Book p44)

questions.sec: Binocular single vision — grades and formation
questions.q: Which statement about antagonistic muscles is FALSE per the book?
opts: They are 2 muscles with opposite action in the same eye
Example: right LR and right MR (abduction and adduction)
Example: right SR and left IO
A lesion of the yoke or antagonist muscles can produce squint
questions.exp: Antagonistic: 2 muscles with opposite action in the same eye (eg right LR and right MR). Right SR + left IO are yoke (version) muscles. (Book p44)

questions.sec: Yoke muscle pairs, Hering's and Sherrington's laws
questions.q: Match the yoke muscle pair with its net action in the book's table — 1) Left LR + right MR 2) Right LR + left MR 3) Right SR + left IO 4) Right IR + left SO … A) Levoversion B) Dextro-elevation C) Dextro-depression D) Dextroversion
questions.exp: Left LR + right MR — levoversion; right LR + left MR — dextroversion; right SR + left IO — dextro-elevation; right IR + left SO — dextro-depression. (Book p45)

questions.sec: Yoke muscle pairs, Hering's and Sherrington's laws
questions.q: All of the following yoke pairs in the book's table produce depression or elevation movements EXCEPT:
opts: Right SR + right IO and left SR + left IO (B/L elevation: sursumversion)
questions.exp: Right SO + left IR — levo-depression; right IO + left SR — levo-elevation; right SR + right IO and left SR + left IO — B/L elevation: sursumversion; right IR + right SO and left IR + left SO — B/L depression: deorsumversion. Levoversion (left LR + right MR) is a horizontal movement. (Book p45)

questions.sec: Yoke muscle pairs, Hering's and Sherrington's laws
questions.q: Hering's law of equal innervation in the book states:
opts: Equal innervation to a pair of yoke muscles
The antagonist always receives less innervation
Only one eye is innervated during version
Innervation decreases with the distance of gaze
questions.exp: Hering's law of equal innervation: equal innervation to a pair of yoke muscles during any binocular movement (similar timing, amount of nerve impulses, simultaneous contraction). (Book p45)

questions.sec: Yoke muscle pairs, Hering's and Sherrington's laws
questions.q: The book lists applications of Hering's law. All of the following belong EXCEPT:
opts: Equal and simultaneous innervation through yoke muscles
questions.exp: Applications: secondary deviation or inhibitional palsy; note: Hering's law — equal and simultaneous innervation flows through yoke muscles. The forced duction test is not an application of Hering's law. (Book p45)

questions.sec: Yoke muscle pairs, Hering's and Sherrington's laws
questions.q: Fill up: Sherrington's law of reciprocal inhibition in the book is the relaxation of the yoke ______.
questions.exp: Sherrington's law of reciprocal inhibition: relaxation of yoke muscle antagonists (eg right MR contracted while right LR relaxed, and the yoke partner mirrors it). (Book p45)

questions.sec: Yoke muscle pairs, Hering's and Sherrington's laws
questions.q: Per the book's BSV formation note, maintaining single vision requires ______ muscles — a yoke pair plus their antagonists; a lesion produces:
questions.exp: Formation of BSV: 4 muscles required — a yoke + antagonists; lesions → squint. (Book p45)

units.title: Squint — definition, causes and the EOM action tables
units.guide: Squint: deviation from binocular vision; overview — deviation of direction of vessels in one/both eyes and impairment in ocular movement. Causes: muscular disorders (myasthenia gravis, atrophy, dystrophy) and cranial nerve lesions (CN IV → superior oblique, CN VI → lateral rectus, CN III → other extraocular muscles; mnemonic SO4LR6O3). Anatomical actions: ability to be free from neural control, based on direction of tendons. Table: LPS — elevation of upper eyelid; MR — inward movement (adduction); LR — outward movement (abduction); cycloducts' 1°/2°/3° actions — SR elevation/intorsion/adduction, IR depression/extorsion/adduction, SO intorsion/depression/abduction, IO extorsion/elevation/abduction. Clinically visible: adduction, abduction, elevation, depression; invisible: intorsion (inward/nasal rotation), extorsion (outward/temporal rotation). Clinical actions: 1° actions predominate in the abducted eye, 2° in the adducted eye; use — to test actions of individual muscles.

units.title: Visual and orbital axes; BSV grades and formation
units.guide: Visual and orbital axes: visual axis–orbital axis 23°; SR and IR muscle axes parallel to the orbital axis at 23° with the sagittal plane; LR muscle axis −45° with the sagittal plane; MR axis parallel to the sagittal plane. If the eye abducts by 23°, the visual axis and the muscle orbital axis coincide → vertical action predominates → SR → pure elevator. Clinical functions: pure elevation SR + IO; pure depression SO + IR; elevation in abduction SR; depression in abduction SO. BSV: formation of a composite image using both the eyes. Grades: 1 — simultaneous macular perception; 2 — fusion of similar images with minute retinal differences; 3 — stereopsis, binocular depth perception. Formation: synergistic muscles (same action, same eye — eg right SR + right IO, both elevation); yoke muscles/CN synergists (one from each eye, same direction — version); antagonistic muscles (opposite action, same eye — eg right LR and right MR).

units.title: Yoke pairs in action, Hering's and Sherrington's laws
units.guide: Yoke pairs and net actions: left LR + right MR — levoversion; right LR + left MR — dextroversion; right SR + left IO — dextro-elevation; right IR + left SO — dextro-depression; right SO + left IR — levo-depression; right IO + left SR — levo-elevation; right SR + right IO and left SR + left IO — B/L elevation (sursumversion); right IR + right SO and left IR + left SO — B/L depression (deorsumversion). Hering's law of equal innervation: equal innervation to a pair of yoke muscles during any binocular movement (similar timing, amount of impulses, simultaneous contraction); applications — secondary deviation or inhibitional palsy. Sherrington's law of reciprocal inhibition: relaxation of yoke muscle antagonists. Formation of BSV: 4 muscles required (a yoke + antagonists); lesions → squint.
